In the printed tradition, are the accents of the Decalogue grammatical?

The question

Roughly speaking, each Decalogue — the one in Exodus and the one in Deuteronomy — has two strands of cantillation, the טעם תחתון and the טעם עליון. Why is this only roughly true? Because in truth there are four strands: at the opening commandment the printed tradition (p-trad) differs from the manuscript tradition (m-trad), yielding two different עליון strands and two different תחתון strands. We have run Richard Goerwitz's accent grammar checker against the m-trad cantillations (as represented by WLC); this page asks the companion question for the p-trad (a tradition still visible in editions like Koren and Simanim): fed through the same grammar checker, are the p-trad's תחתון and עליון grammatical too?

There is no dual cantillation to detangle here. Whereas the Tiberian manuscripts (and WLC) pack both of their strands onto one set of letters, the Wikisource page עשרת הדברות בסיס/טעמים spells out all the strands separately — p-trad and m-trad alike — each as single cantillation. Every chanted verse (delimited by its own sof pasuq) is grammar-checked on its own. The m-trad is the baseline — MAM's own authoritative text, expected to parse clean throughout — and the p-trad is the object of study.

The verdict

Manuscript traditionPrinted tradition
Ex. תחתון✓ all 12 clean✓ all 13 clean
Ex. עליון✓ all 10 clean✗ 1 of 9 ungrammatical (verse 1)
Deut. תחתון✓ all 12 clean✓ all 13 clean
Deut. עליון✓ all 10 clean✗ 1 of 9 ungrammatical (verse 1)

The תחתון is grammatical everywhere — both books, both traditions. The p-trad תחתון differs from the m-trad in details that do not touch the accent grammar (vocalization such as תִּרְצַח vs תִּרְצָח at לא תרצח, and where a maqaf or ga‘ya falls), and in one verse boundary: the p-trad תחתון ends its first verse at מבית עבדים (so it has one more verse than the m-trad, which runs the first two commandments together). Both parse clean.

The עליון is grammatical in the m-trad but not in the p-trad: the p-trad עליון of each Decalogue has exactly one ungrammatical chanted verse — its opening one.

The four strands of אנכי…עבדים

The m-trad and p-trad accent the Decalogue's אנכי…עבדים unit differently. The accent on עבדים is what decides the structure: a silluq + sof pasuq there ends the verse, so אנכי…עבדים stands as its own verse; an etnaḥta or revia there is mid-verse, folding אנכי…עבדים into a longer verse. The table below lays all four strands over the same milestone words — אנכי (their common start), then עבדים, על־פני, and מצותי — so their subset relation is plain: every verse starts green at אנכי and ends red at its own last word, the shorter ones stopping where the longer ones keep going. Each strand keeps its own accent on עבדים, the structure-deciding mark:

mTאנכי֙עבד֑יםעל־פנֽי׃
mE/pTאנכ֖יעבדֽים׃
pEאנכי֙עבד֗יםעל־פנ֗ימצותֽי׃

How many chanted verses each strand divides the Exodus Decalogue into:

strandverse count
m-trad תחתון12
m-trad עליון10
p-trad תחתון13
p-trad עליון9
  • P-trad תחתון = m-trad עליון — but only in the first chanted verse. Once אנכי…עבדים is its own verse there is only one grammatical way to accent it — etnaḥta in the middle, silluq at the end — so in that verse both traditions land on the same marks (consonants, accents, and accent-boundary marks: sof pasuq, maqaf, legarmeh). They differ only by an immaterial meteg (which the stripped cells above drop), so the table gives them a single shared row, labelled mE/pT. The equality stops there: past this first verse the two strands diverge completely — the p-trad תחתון runs the Exodus Decalogue on for 13 chanted verses, the m-trad עליון for only 10.
  • P-trad עליון ≠ m-trad עליון. The p-trad עליון puts revia on עבדים and runs the first two commandments together into one verse (→ 9 total), where the m-trad עליון closes on silluq (→ 10).
  • The m-trad תחתון does not give אנכי…עבדים its own verse either — it runs אנכי…פני together (etnaḥta at עבדים, sof pasuq at פני), a third structure again.

Only one of these four strands is ungrammatical — the p-trad עליון, whose merged opening verse the section below dissects.

Why the p-trad עליון fails: the merged first verse

In the m-trad עליון, the first commandment אָנֹכִי … עֲבָדִים is its own chanted verse, and לא יהיה לך אלהים אחרים begins the next — two separate verses, both of which parse clean. The p-trad instead merges the first two commandments into a single verse (nine chanted verses in all, against the m-trad’s ten). That one merged verse is what the grammar rejects. Shown stripped to consonants and accents (MAM-simple style) and divided at the p-trad תחתון’s verse boundaries — one עליון verse (E) spanning the five ordinary תחתון verses (T) it merges:

Eאנכי֙…מצותֽי׃
Tאנכ֖י…עבדֽים׃לא־יהי֥ה…על־פנֽי׃לא־תעש֨ה…לאֽרץ׃לא־תשתחו֥ה…לשנאֽי׃וע֥שה…מצותֽי׃
e
t

The single etnaḥta falls at לְשֹׂנְאָי, leaving an over-long first half that has a segolta plus three separate revia domains (at עֲבָדִים, עַל־פָּנַי, and לָאָרֶץ); the prose grammar cannot build it and returns a pashta_phrase error — the same failure, at the same structural point, in both Decalogues.

The cause is the merged structure, not sheer length: Deuteronomy’s p-trad עליון Sabbath verse runs 55 words and parses clean, while this merged verse (51 words) does not. Keeping the two commandments as the m-trad’s two separate verses (9 and 42 words) is exactly what lets them parse.
